raw_response:
Aiya, you want to know my plan this year? Let me think through it, field by field.

---

My old man and I, we're the only ones left here. Kids went to the city long ago. 33 mu is a lot for two old people, but we manage, same as always. About 10 mu I keep for cotton — the western field, sandy soil, always been cotton there. The other 23 mu is wheat and corn, one after the other, no rest for the land.

**Wheat first, because that's what's in the ground now, or going in soon.** I plant around National Day time, early October. The seed I buy from the co-op in town, same kind the village uses — old Wang next door, Li family across, we all plant about the same. No fancy seed, the expensive ones aren't for us. Before planting I put down compound fertilizer, maybe two big bags over about 10 mu, you know, the 15-15-15 kind from the shop. When the wheat stands up in spring and starts jointing, I spread urea, about one bag for every five or six mu. That's what I've always done. Water in winter before the ground freezes, water at jointing, water once more before harvest if it doesn't rain. If heaven gives rain, I skip — pumping costs money, the well meter runs fast.

**Then corn goes in right after wheat comes off in June.** No time to rest, maybe three days to clear the straw and plant. We use the little seeder, push it by hand down the rows. Seed from whatever the shop is pushing that year — I can't read the bags, my husband asks the shopkeeper. Fertilizer same idea, compound at planting, urea when the corn is knee-high. Summer has rain usually, so maybe only water once if July is dry. Yield is about 400-some kg per mu, same as the neighbors.

**Cotton is the hard one.** Plant end of April when the ground warms. I use the hybrid seed my cousin told me about years back, works fine. Cotton doesn't need as much fertilizer as corn, but it needs spraying — the bollworm eats everything if you don't. The agro-shop man tells us what to buy. The worst is picking in autumn. My back isn't what it was. I hire three or four neighbor women for a few days, 100 yuan a day, and we pick together. Otherwise cotton would rot in the field.

Money is tight. Whatever I spend on fertilizer, I can't spend on medicine or the grandson's new year money. So I don't go overboard. Last year was okay, so this year I'll do about the same. If something is broken I fix it, but I don't change what isn't broken.
